title: Track a drifting conveyor belt back to center at the tail take-ups: at most a quarter turn per two belt revolutions
instruction: The belt on this conveyor is running off to one side. Fix it before it rubs the frame.
context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (O*NET 49-9041.00, 49-9043.00, 49-9044.00) track belts daily in packaging, food and distribution plants. A belt does not move the moment an adjuster turns: it walks over the next few revolutions, toward the side of the pulley with less tension. So the trade tracks at the tail take-ups in steps of at most a quarter turn and watches several revolutions before the next (Texas Belting), until the belt is within a quarter inch of center (Hytrol). Cranking a screw several turns, or turning the wrong one, runs the belt into the frame, where its edge frays, and it can tear and throw product; over-tightening both sides overloads the bearings and splice. Unlike tasks where a lag is learned once on a sample, here a live process is steered while it keeps drifting. Left alone, this belt reaches the frame in about 20 seconds.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A benchtop flat-belt conveyor (a 1:2 model of a light-duty slider-bed conveyor) is fixed on the table with its belt running along +y at 20 cm/s. Two extruded aluminum side frames, 1 cm thick, stand along x 19.5 to 20.5 and 35.5 to 36.5 from y -4.7 to 28.2, z 5 to 11, on four dark legs; their inner faces are 15 cm apart. Between them a steel slider bed carries the black belt's top run at z 10, 13 cm wide, so it clears each frame by 1 cm and the frames stand 1 cm above it as edge guides. The 74 cm belt loop turns on two 4 cm pulleys with axes along x at z 8: the tail pulley at y -3.5 (the robot's right) and the head pulley at y 27, driven by a dark gear motor outside the far frame at x 39.5, y 27. The belt shows yellow chevrons every 6 cm moving with it and a white center stripe; a white mark on the tail guard shows the frame's center line at x 28, and beside it a belt-edge sensor's bar of 21 LEDs (6 mm apart, x 22 to 34) lights the one green LED at the belt's offset to the nearest mm, the middle one when centered. Yellow sheet guards cover both pulley nips (top at z 11.8). Tail take-ups: on each side the tail pulley's bearing block is drawn by an M10 x 1.5 adjusting screw lying along y at z 8, at x 19 (near side) and x 37 (far side), through a steel end plate at y -7.3 bolted to the frame. Each screw ends in a blue four-lobe knob, 3.4 cm across the lobes and 2.8 cm long, from y -7.7 to -10.5, with a white index mark on its top lobe; turning a knob clockwise as seen from its end draws that end of the pulley outward by 1.5 mm per turn, up to 2 turns either way in its slot. At the start the belt runs 2 mm toward the far frame (x +) and the tail pulley sits 0.75 mm out of square (the far end half a turn short), so the belt is drifting toward the far frame. Its tension is the set 0.5 percent stretch. Both arms start at their ready pose; nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The belt's sideways offset from the frame's center line follows the tracking law in the README (a skewed pulley steers the belt toward its slacker end, lagged by one revolution, with crowned-pulley centering). e is the larger of the offset at the end and where the belt settles with the screws as left. 0 (irreversible): the belt's edge reached a side frame (10 mm off center, its clearance) at any moment, even if tracked back after; or a screw was backed out of its bearing block (more than 2 turns loosened); or more than 0.3 turn of adjustment, both screws together, within any 7.4 s (Texas Belting's quarter turn at a time plus 18 degrees of slip, then several revolutions: 7.4 s is two of this belt's), a screw turned out and back counting its whole excursion. 0: a gripper holds a knob at the end or a tool point or pad tip is within 4 cm of any part of a knob (a finger's width plus the arm's lag); the edge moved 0.1 mm/s or more at any step of the last 10 s (still drifting; 1 mm in 10 s is under what a ruler shows); e over 6 mm (half an inch at the model's 1:2 scale). 0.25: e 3 to 6 mm (running clear, off center), or e within 3 mm with the belt's stretch outside 0.3 to 0.8 percent (too slack: the drive slips; too tight: splice and bearings overloaded; set at 0.5). 1.0: e within 3 mm (Hytrol's quarter inch at 1:2), steady, stretch in the window, knobs let go, both arms home and still; 0.9 if an arm is not home. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.9, 1.0. Do nothing, the wrong screw or one big crank end in a rub: 0; the whole half-turn fix in one go, or two quarter turns closer than two revolutions, is rushed: 0. Real trial: the edge sensor's reading and a ruler across the tail at the center mark at the end and after 2 more minutes of running, masking tape on the frames' inner faces for a rub (and the video), the knobs' index marks for the turns made.
reset_notes: Stop the belt. Set both knobs to their paint marks, back the far one off half a turn, center the belt by hand, start the conveyor and begin the trial when the belt's edge passes the 2 mm mark toward the far frame. A trial that rubs scuffs the masking tape on the frame's inner face and the belt edge: replace the tape; a frayed belt edge is per-trial wear and the belt is replaced when it shows.
fidelity: The belt is not a physical body: its sideways offset follows a scored law (steering v x skew toward the slack end, one-revolution lag, crowned-pulley centering, time constant 16 s, 6.7 mm per quarter turn), drawn as a moving texture. Its constants are the model's, to be calibrated on the real conveyor (README). Tension is the loop's stretch only; no load or slip. The knobs turn on modeled screws with light resistance, and the whole conveyor is at 1:2 scale.
